title: Introduction to WordPress
objectives: Choose Posts versus Pages for school content.
introduction: Develop introduction to wordpress using a real authorized WordPress environment. CodeLab provides instructions and evidence review, not a WordPress installation.
explanation: WordPress is a Content Management System. Editors manage content in a dashboard; a theme presents it to visitors. Domains provide an address and hosting supplies server resources. Blogs, business/school sites, portfolios, news sites and stores use different content models. WordPress.org distributes self-hosted software; WordPress.com is a hosted service with plan-dependent capabilities. Their plugin/theme controls are not identical. Posts are dated entries grouped by categories/tags; Pages hold persistent information. Themes control presentation, plugins add functionality and Media stores assets. Dashboard and admin-toolbar controls depend on role and installed features.

Record WordPress version, theme type and approved plugins. WordPress.com plan limits may differ. Use an authorized local/staging/school practice site and fictional data. Back up before significant changes; never risk important production sites. Do not upload passwords, API keys, database configuration, private academic information or unredacted backup archives.

2. Sign in using your assigned account without copying credentials into CodeLab.

3. Locate Posts, Pages and Media; inspect one item in each.

4. Locate Appearance and identify the active theme and available tools.

5. Locate Plugins, Users and Settings if permitted; record unavailable controls rather than requesting unnecessary privileges.

6. Inspect the visitor site and create a redacted map of the seven dashboard areas.

Distinguish publishing states and media descriptions.
introduction: Develop creating pages, posts, and media using a real authorized WordPress environment. CodeLab provides instructions and evidence review, not a WordPress installation.

title: Using the Block Editor
objectives: Build an About page with common blocks.
introduction: Develop using the block editor using a real authorized WordPress environment. CodeLab provides instructions and evidence review, not a WordPress installation.
explanation: The Block Editor, often called Gutenberg, composes Paragraph, Heading, Image, Gallery, Columns, Buttons, List, Table and Cover blocks. Group organizes related blocks; Spacer adds space but should not substitute for sensible layout. List View exposes nested structure and reading order; block settings differ from document settings. Patterns reuse layouts; synced-pattern edits can affect every synchronized use. Use heading semantics rather than font size alone, descriptive links and tables for tabular data. Columns must stack in a sensible order on narrow screens.

important_notes: Common errors: assuming identical theme/version menus; checking only as Administrator; using real private data; claiming success without inspecting the visitor result. debugging_tip: Reproduce on the authorized practice site with fictional data. Record expected/actual result, menu route, role, theme and plugin versions. Check permissions and capabilities before changes; keep a rollback point and escalate recovery to the owner.

accessibility_tip: Use logical headings, contextual image alt text, descriptive links, labeled fields, readable contrast and keyboard-operable navigation. Check focus and reading order; a theme/plugin choice alone is not proof of accessibility.
responsive_tip: Test actual content at mobile, tablet and desktop widths: menu operation, column stacking, media scaling, table/form overflow, readable text and touch controls. Document one correction.
maintenance_tip: Assign backup/update ownership, keep necessary components maintained, verify compatibility on staging and protect retained backups. Record actual restoration tests or state explicitly that restoration remains untested.
